extracted.intended_audience: students of journalism, media historians, and newspaper professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and historical standards for newspaper content, page make-up, reporting styles, and production technologies (front-page design, leads, columns, pictures, comics, newsgathering and transmission) as practiced in American newspapers 1914–1940.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of front-page banners to stimulate sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Front-page banners were used widely during the World War and continued because of their value in stimulating street sales; many papers used them every day whether the available news seemed to demand them or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Banners can increase visibility and street sales, but typographical excellence contests showed best front pages often avoided conventional black gothic banners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical excellence: multi-line heads in caps and lower-case
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemplary front pages (e.g., New York Herald Tribune, 1931) commonly used three-line heads two and three columns wide set in caps and lower-case—a make-up that gained favor and contrasted with the black gothic streamer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For typographic quality prefer three-line heads in caps & lower-case and avoid heavy gothic banners which can reduce aesthetic excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined make-up
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘stream-lined make-up’ involved omission of column rules, 'monkey dashes,' and multiple decks of heads; it required setting heads flush left in caps and lower-case of non-serif types—opening up and lightening the typographical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a cleaner page by removing visual clutter and using flush-left, non-serif headline treatments to modernize appearance; note that not all papers adopted the full technique, but its influence was significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmentalization and front-page summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: There was a tendency to departmentalize news and to print general summaries on the front page; some papers gave considerable front-page space to news summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize front-page content into departments and include concise summaries to help readers navigate complex news flows—useful for local adaptation of national/interpretive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead style: move beyond the standard 5W-H summary lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the influence of radio newscasting, Time, and emphasis on interpretation, feature leads with greater variety and more instant appeals to reader-interest became common by 1940, replacing the standard 5W-H summary lead in many places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use more varied, attention-getting feature leads that aim for immediate reader interest rather than strict 5W-H formula; balance immediacy with factual accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of interpretation in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing complexity of economic, social, and international news forced some retreat from purely factual reporting; interpretation of the facts was presented chiefly in three ways: (1) interpolated paragraphs or sentences in a news story (set in italics or within brackets/parentheses), (2) editorialized reports under a by-line, and (3) signed correspondence of commentators or columnists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adding interpretation, clearly differentiate it from straight reporting (typographic cues, by-lines) to avoid blurring into undisclosed opinion; be mindful that interpretation can easily become editorial comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and value of by-line stories and signed columns
rubrics_metrics.description: The growing importance of by-line stories and signed columns signaled a recrudescence of personal journalism; ace reporters and columnists, not editors, increasingly stood for their papers and built reputations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By-lines and signed commentary can increase credibility and reader attachment; ensure author accountability and distinguish opinion from news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gossip column practice and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The gossip column pioneered by Winchell brought intimate gossip about private persons into daily columns—covering matters like personal relationships and pregnancies—which attracted readers but raised reputation and libel/privacy concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gossip can draw readers but carries legal/ethical risks (libel, invasions of privacy); exercise verification, restraint, and consider reputation impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of political columns and their risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Two political-column types developed: (a) the sober syndicated forum by known publicists, and (b) 'dope and gossip' columns purporting behind-the-scenes information. The latter could deteriorate into undependable keyhole journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sober, evidence-based political columns support public discourse; behind-the-scenes gossip columns may attract attention but risk inaccuracy and loss of trust—editors should monitor standards and sourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of comics due to high reader interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Gallup surveys showed comic strips had higher reader interest than any other features and higher than most news; publishers commonly preserved comics even while cutting other features during the Depression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given strong audience engagement, comics are a priority feature for readership retention; cutting them is likely to harm circulation more than cutting other features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for continuity (serial) comic strips and popular strip types
rubrics_metrics.description: The older gag strips gave way to continuity strips (serial adventure and superman phases) in the 1920s, though humor swung back by 1940; many long-running popular strips originated in this era.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serial storytelling in comics can sustain regular readership; editors should consider balance between continuity and gag strips to match audience tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Big-play editorial technique: prioritize human-interest drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors often gave a promising story 'a big play'—using strong human elements, drama, and suspense—to the point of crowding other matters off the front page, because such play boosted circulation and competitors would follow suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize stories with clear human-interest and drama for circulation gains, but remain aware of risks that important but less sensational items may be underplayed; balance editorial judgment and public service obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness categories for 'great stories'
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine 'great news stories' commonly related to wars, presidential elections, great disasters, dramatic or sensational crimes, and popular or 'built up' sports events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories as heuristics for allocating resources and front-page space, but avoid mechanically equating prominence with civic importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radio newscasting limits and agency concessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Early A.P. rules forbade broadcasting of its members' news; in 1925 rules relaxed to allow use of news 'of transcendent national or international importance'; in 1928 A.P., U.P., and I.N.S. agreed to give radio two daily broadcasts and later allowed sale of news to stations; A.P. did not allow use of its reports on sponsored newscasts until 1939.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When providing content to broadcasters, distinguish between types of news allowed and commercial sponsorship constraints; negotiate agency rights mindful of exclusivity and fair use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of transmission technologies (teletypes, teletypesetters, wirephoto, telephotography)
rubrics_metrics.description: The teletypewriter and teletypesetter greatly increased wire speed and capacity, replacing Morse-code telegraphy; wirephoto (telephotography) services from the mid-1920s–1930s enabled rapid transmission of pictures; rotogravure and multicolor presses enhanced picture supplements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt technologies that speed transmission (teletype), enable picture delivery (wirephoto), and improve reproduction (rotogravure) to expand news and picture capability—consider costs (presses, equipment) and potential for wider picture saturation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of special newsgathering resources (airplanes, photographers, agencies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Airplanes, news photographers, and picture agencies (Wide World Photos, Associated Press Picture Service, Acme, International News Photos) became important for gathering and distributing visuals; photographers' intrusiveness sometimes caused conflicts and privacy invasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy specialized resources (aerial photography, picture services) to secure unique visual coverage, but train staff on privacy, law enforcement interaction, and ethical boundaries to avoid legal and reputational harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing picture saturation and supplements
rubrics_metrics.description: Picture use rose sharply (tabloids filling up to 40% of non-advertising space), reaching possible saturation by late 1930s; improvements in photography, engraving, and presses both caused and resulted from the flood of pictures; weeklies like Life and Look exploited pictorial demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance visual content with editorial needs; excessive picture saturation may reach limits—ensure pictures serve storytelling and not merely fill space; invest in reproduction capabilities for quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of polling and reader-interest measurement (Gallup method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gallup developed sampling methods for gauging reader interest and public opinion; his Institute (founded 1935) accurately measured opinion by sampling, improving on flawed straw-vote approaches (e.g., Literary Digest failure in 1936); initial errors were ~6.5%, later claimed around 3%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scientifically designed sampling surveys to inform editorial decisions and measure reader interest; avoid unrepresentative straw polls and understand margins of error when interpreting results.
